To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) The impact of local features on storm surge propagation is dependent on storm characteristics, 2) The impact of bottom friction on storm surges is dependent on local characteristics and storm characteristics, and 3) The impact of mesh resolution on storm surges propagation is dependent on the storm characteristics, local features and the location in the model domain.

(a) storm surge attenuation rates for weak to moderate events in wetlands are highly dependent on local topographic features and the exposure of the wetland to surge; (b) storm surge attenuation in wetlands is greatly diminished by stronger storms; (c) storm surge attenuation is highly dependent on the mesh resolution used in the model; (d) the impact of bottom friction is minimal for storm surge modeling; (e) storm surge attenuation for weaker events is greater for smaller storms, while for

1) the attenuation rate of surge through small scale wetland areas in a barrier island system is dependent on storm strength, and 2) for weak to moderate storm conditions the attenuation rate of the back bays system is influenced secondarily by local geomorphological features.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding and quantifying the impact of wetlands and barrier islands in the attenuation of storm surge.
understanding how the local topography, wetland characteristics and inlet configurations impact surge attenuation and inundation extent in the Delmarvian wetland systems.
the evaluation of the impact of spatial resolution, storm intensity and storm characteristics on storm surge propagation in the wetland areas of the Mid-Attlantic coast.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
wetlands and barrier islands do provide a measure of storm surge attenuation, but this mitigation is highly dependent on local features and the strength of the storm.
the role of wetland attenuation of storm surge is a function of storm characteristics, local bathymetry/topography, and the presence and configuration of barrier islands and inlets.
the attenuation rates observed in this study are highly dependent on storm characteristics and local features and therefore cannot be generalized for all wetland areas in similar coastal regions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the impact of storm surge on the wetlands of the Delmarvian Peninsula is highly dependent on the storm characteristics, local bathymetry, and the configuration of the barrier island system, and therefore, the use of a single attenuation rate for the region would not be recommended.

for weak storms, the attenuation of surge through wetland areas can be significant and can be used to estimate a mitigation rate for a particular area; however, the attenuation rate for a stronger storm is not as significant and can vary greatly depending on the local characteristics of the wetland system.
the use of a storm attenuation index for storm surge in wetlands should be done with caution and only after a detailed evaluation of the local characteristics and the expected storm characteristics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
storm characteristics, such as forward speed, size, duration and central low pressure, are more influential than local characteristics, such as wetland extent, in the attenuation of storm surge.

the use of a single index for storm surge attenuation may be insufficient to capture the full complexity of the coastal system, especially when considering the impact of extreme events on coastal resiliency.
storm surge attenuation by wetlands and coastal ecosystems is not a constant and is not necessarily a linear function of wetlands area.
